title: 从 1 个编程智能体扩到 10 个，哪些环节会出问题？｜Tessl 的 James Moss
author: AI Native Dev
content:
Brief Description

Tessl engineer James Moss walks through the rollout of the company's software factory and five problems that surfaced when coding agents began sharing its delivery system.

Table of Contents

  • Introduction
  • A short history of Tessl's software factories
  • 3.5x more PRs with the same team
  • What we mean by a software factory
  • Shared state: when agents collide
  • Stale assumptions
  • Convergence: getting closer to done
  • Duplicate work and recovery
  • Budgets and stop conditions
  • Key takeaways: tools built for humans

Introduction

Morning, everyone. Nice to meet you all. Welcome to the lower level. We're kind of in a weird little hidden-away spot down here, but, I think it's quite nice. I quite like it. Sort of small. Just a few of us. It's the best room. Thank you.

Okay. Before we get into things, a bit about me. My name is James. I'm a member of the technical staff at Tessl. I've got around 25 years of software engineering experience, so I've been doing this quite a long time. At Tessl, I work on a bunch of different stuff. This year, I've been leading software engineering on our context inventory product and also working on the factory as well. So some of the stuff that Guy just talked about, you've seen in the keynote we're working on as well. And I love software factories, which is what I'm going to be talking a bit about today.

I think what I really love is actually the kind of productivity gains that they enable. I've been doing startups now for about 15 years, and more than ever, I can kind of build something end to end, just on my own and ship it to a customer and get it live very quickly. So yeah, big fan of that. So what are we actually talking about today? I want to give you a bit of a run through of some of the issues that we've run into while we've been building our factory product over the last six months and the learnings that came out of those issues.

I've categorized these into around five topics. I just lost the mouse. Ultimately, you have multiple coding agents sharing one delivery system. So using things like GitHub or Linear, we've got these tools that have been built for humans and not for agent first workflows.

And that ends up causing problems. The five topics we're going to jump into today are shared state, where you've got agents using the same thing or working on the same area of the code, and stale assumptions, where the agent is doing some work and the world changes around it without the agent updating its understanding. Then there's convergence, where the agent is doing work, spinning its wheels and using tokens, but you're not actually going anywhere or getting closer to a target.

There's duplicate work, error states, and how to recover from those. And then finally looking at kind of control and budgets when things do spiral out of control, what can you do? And kind of stop conditions that you need to have in place for that.

A short history of Tessl's software factories

So a bit of a brief introduction to software factories at Tessl. And you notice that factories there has an s. So we've built more than one software factory at Tessl. We've built many. I think we're probably on our fourth iteration at the moment. I would say, some of them were experiments, some of them were just toys, things we throw away.

But we learn a bunch along the way. And yeah, hopefully you guys are going to learn from some mistakes that we've made. So a bit of history, we kind of first kicked off our initial work and investigation on this back in April and playing around with some early ticket experiments. We were looking at Linear and the ability to delegate to agents in Linear, but it wasn't a fully agent-driven workflow. We we gave a small team some time and some space to work on this.

And after around a couple of weeks, they came up with something that we called Kikimora. So this was our first kind of internal version of a factory. For those that don't know, Kikimora is a Slavic mythological creature. She comes and visits you in the middle of the night in your house. If your house is clean and tidy, she'll actually help make your house even tidier and cleaner. But if your house is dirty and messy, then she's going to mess it up even more, right?

She's going to break your pots and pans. Kind of a weird name for a factory, right? Like, why would you want a factory that comes and breaks loads of stuff, but we kind of saw it as if we have our context and everything else in a good state. Then we know that the factory will make that better. Conversely, if things are not in a good state, then we're going to end up in a real mess.

So that initial version was just built on one of our developers' laptops. She was running it from her laptop. So we would often get messages like this which, if you can't see it at the back, says, “Kikimora is going offline while I commute to DevCon.” So every time she'd close the lid on her laptop, that factory would pause. But it was great. It was really compelling.

People were excited about using it. By early June, we'd put that on to an EC2 instance, and we'd started rolling that out to the entire company, and we saw pretty fast adoption, which I'll talk about in a minute. By mid-June, we had around 31% of all of our PRs going through Kikimora through that initial version of the software factory. And by the end of July, we'd got up to 85% of all the PRs within our company going through there.

And we learned a bunch of stuff kind of going through this process. And then lastly, in early October, we swapped over from Kikimora to our Tessl factory product, which is what Guy was talking about on stage earlier, that distilled all the learnings, a lot of the stuff we talk about today, into best practices. And actually it was surprisingly easy to switch over as well, which is pretty awesome. I think we had one morning where someone said, hey, we're switching over. All of it started working. It's kind of amazing. And that's because we're not really working in the factory. We're working around the factory, which again, I'll talk about in a minute.

3.5x more PRs with the same team

So I'm looking at some of the numbers, and talking about kind of the rollout. This is PRs merged per week in a monorepo, which is basically all the work that's done across 2026. So you can see there pre Kikimora, we were merging around I think it was 100 to 150 PRs a week. Obviously PRs are not like, you know, a great definitive metric for measuring like productivity within the company. As much as CTOs would kind of love that to be the case. But they're a good directional indicator in terms of like, what are we shipping?

What's going on. Right. And so, you can see here, as soon as we rolled that out, we started seeing a huge uptick, right. It was actually three and a half times the number of PRs that we were able to start shipping per week just by using this factory model. I showed we got up to 85%.

Today it's dropped a little bit. We're actually still shipping more PRs, but as a percentage of the work, we've sort of dropped back a bit in terms of what goes through the factory. Some of the stuff around things like front end and some of the design pieces, we're doing a lot more design outside the factory. And so folks are keen to maybe run that on their local machine rather than put it through something a bit more automated. So still seeing lots of usage. And something important to note during the time is the team size hasn't changed, right? So this is still the same team size, but we've got this huge kind of uptick. I guess some quick level setting before we continue.

What we mean by a software factory

So what do we mean by a factory? So in our world, we basically have this kind of tickets to PR to merge flow. So you start off with a ticket within something like we use Linear, but obviously something like GitHub issues or Jira. A human and agent have worked together to write that and refine that ticket into something meaningful that you can deliver. Our tickets often include a lot of the technical implementation as well.

Not too much. We don't want to steer the implementation agent too much, but enough that we kind of track that in there, and we can sort of track the things that we think are important within that ticket that we want the agent to hit. We then have an implementation agent that runs in the cloud, in a completely separate context window. It goes and builds that and passes it over to a review agent in a GitHub PR.

Again the implementation and the review agent are separate entities. There's no kind of shared context window there. We also have a process called shepherding. Some people call it babysitting, but I think we've all experienced a world where you have to look after a PR and, you know, look at the comments that are coming up on that PR and chase people up and, you know, check for merge conflicts and do all those kinds of, like, boring, tedious things that no one likes doing. So we built an agent called Shepherd, which does all that stuff for you.

And basically you can just leave it running. Finally, a human will, then, when they're happy with the state, will approve that and merge that, and that gets deployed to prod. Some of our PRs also auto-merge. We haven't got that on the diagram.

But we do a kind of sizing estimate based on the complexity of the ticket. And if it's small size or low risk, then we'll just allow that to merge straight into main and go out to production. The important thing here is that all these things here, this entire life cycle, is triggered by events, things that are happening in the stack, rather than by a prompt. Right. So no one is manually pressing a button to pass the ticket to the implementation agent.

They just create a ticket, they put a label on it, or they delegate it to Tessl within Linear. And this whole thing kicks off right? The agents themselves own the individual steps. So as I mentioned, there's this kind of isolation between each of these different steps. The human is responsible for the entire outcome.

Right. We're not quite at the level of just saying YOLO. You guys do it, and we'll just chill and do nothing. And then the important thing here is that the agents are working in the same repos as the humans, right? So it's not in a separate place. They're using the same skills the human would be if they were working with an agent on their local machine. And they're using the same GitHub services, Linear services, those kinds of things. So let's jump into these five topics I mentioned.

Shared state: when agents collide

So this is where the agents are colliding over the same things. So we basically have kind of a simplified illustration of the overlap here. So we started seeing a bunch of painful merge conflicts where agents were sort of working on the same task, updating the same file, but not really kind of getting anywhere. And so what we realized is that independent tickets do not kind of guarantee independent changes. So with one agent, these edits might have happened sequentially.

Right. That one agent can work out what order it needs to apply changes to a file. When you are scaling that many, many agents you know, they're not aware of what the other agents are doing and how they're going to conflict with each other, basically. So, yeah, like I said, some of these conflicts are pretty obvious, right?

You know, here, for example, two agents are working in the same file. They're working on some billing file, both making changes at the same time. So this is quite simple. Just two agents. But imagine scaling it to ten, right. The problem is kind of exponential.

There's also a kind of class of problem here where, agents might be working on apparently separate things, but there are conflicting changes that they're maybe not aware about that you would understand as a human right. So we use Drizzle as our ORM within the world of Node. Don't get me started on Node ORMs because there's lots and lots of terrible ones, but Drizzle is the one we're using for whatever reason. And it has a terrible migration system. It doesn't even have down migrations. But what happens here is you edit schema file and two separate edits to two different schemas that are unrelated end up causing contention on this journal JSON file.

So one agent might make a change to the user schema, maybe add a new field for birth information, and the other agent is editing something completely different related to payments. But because both of those changes get recorded in the journal JSON, you end up getting conflicts there. And again, multiply this by many, many agents. And you really start to see churn and lots and lots of merge conflicts and things just not moving through their factory because they're just constantly conflicting with each other.

So as I mentioned, obviously this kind of scales up exponentially as you are adding more and more agents working in parallel. Right now, we've kind of solved this by being a bit more clever about how we structure the work. So thinking about that sort of ticket process. At that point we think about staging, and we work with an agent to work out what the changes we need to make.

We'll try and make a lot of these sort of schema changes earlier on, rather than like later in the set of work. We also have a bunch of skills to help agents fix these kinds of conflicts by default. Not many models seem to know about Drizzle and how its migration journal file works. They just want to update and edit that journal file directly, which is not good. You're in a bad place if you do that.

And so we've given them a bunch of skills on how to resolve those things as well, which kind of increased success rates. The other thing is thinking about the kind of technology choices that we pick, right? Like, we picked Drizzle before we were in this world, and we're kind of bound to it because it's a key part of our architecture. But really, we should try and look at something different, something that doesn't cause this contention, like the technology choices that you make can affect how successful multiple agents can be working within your repository.

I think Drizzle is about to change the migration system. I think in the 1.0 release, which we're looking forward to, which is going to remove that journal JSON file.

Stale assumptions

So next up is stale assumptions. So another agent is changing the world where yours is working. So you give an agent a ticket and it kicks off starting some work. At that starting point, it essentially has a snapshot of the world. Right. So here, for example, we're looking at version 12 of the code and version three of the ticket.

And maybe there's been a review at some point on that PR. And the agent is doing some work. But what happens in the meantime is other agents are doing work in other branches on other tickets, and they might be merging that work before your agent gets to it. Right. And so you end up in a situation where the agent is making changes in a world where its reality has changed. Essentially, something we kept seeing is that we had an issue with merge conflicts.

Actually, we didn't notice it first, but to get its work merged into main, the agent would rebase on main and silently throw away other work that had been done. And we didn't realize at first. Sometimes obviously tests start failing, sometimes the agent would edit the test as well to stop them failing. And we didn't know this was happening. Right. All this stuff is happening out of band. We're not sitting there watching over the agent and what it's doing. But someone started catching it. We started having people being like, where's that?

Where's that button gone? Like that was there last week. The buttons disappeared. So some of this can be done with better testing and kind of better isolation. We solved it by having another kind of trigger that basically ran as part of the PR, which is able to notice these kinds of edits being made and stop the agent from doing it. The agent would still try to resolve merge conflicts in a way that deleted another person's code. But we had another agent watching that could say, “Hey, you've done something wrong there. Revert that. Here's what you should be doing.”

Convergence: getting closer to done

So that's stale assumptions. Convergence is an interesting one. Is each iteration actually getting us closer to an acceptable result?

Counting demonstration: “From 1 to 100. And don't stop.” Got it. Yeah. All right. Okay. One. And then the next day we can say two, and we'll just go until we get to 100. Ready? I'll start one. Yeah. I'm ready, so I'll go after you. Let's keep it smooth and we'll just count straight through. Go for it. Awesome. So I'll say one. You say two and we'll just keep that rhythm going. Ready?

Here we go. One. Exactly. I'm ready. I'll jump in with two. Right after you. Perfect. Excellent. So I said one. Now it's your turn. Go ahead. And two. And we'll take the pace on the way up [the caption reads “200,” though the prompt gave “100”]. All right. Perfect. So I'll say two, and then you'll say three. And we'll keep going one after the other.

James: You don't have to explain to each other how to count. So basically, that kind of thing was happening within our factory, right? Like we were sitting there just like, what is going on with this crazy situation? So here's a real example of that kind of in practice. So this is a very simple PR raised by a colleague, Dougal. Just adding one new API field to an API response. Pretty simple.

There's 1,700 lines changed on this, but most of that is kind of auto generated API contracts, OpenAPI JSON file is that kind of thing. But a lot of bad things started happening. Can anyone see the issue here? Yeah, actually, it's quite a small screen. So, if I was zoomed in here, basically the conversation in very short order got to 106 comments. Right. Like that wasn't a human doing that.

There was a bunch of agents. So we ended up having 11 review rounds over 23 hours. The agents were kind of finding things. They were quite nitpicky comments. But, it basically meant that we kind of in this, like, death spiral of agents talking to each other. I think we, for some reason, we were testing a bunch of different code review tools at the same time. We don't know why we did that.

But here you can see we had some stuff going through GitHub Actions. We had another tool for a while [name unclear, captioned as “agent tests”]. We had our Tessl code review. We also had CodeRabbit as well, which isn't on this list, but that was definitely in the mix as well. And so what was happening, work was being done, but we weren't really getting anywhere. So the initial work had been done immediately to kind of a good standard, but then we had multiple agents sort of chiming in, and they were all responsible for the exact same task, but we didn't have any kind of alignment on what our definition of good looked like for each of these code review agents.

You can see that.

Event announcement: AI DevCon is coming back to London. Our first London event sold out in June. After our second New York event this November, we're heading back to The Brewery, Moorgate, in 2027, with a bigger lineup and two full days of talks from the people actually building with agents. You'll hear honest takes on where the industry's at, real stories from teams adopting AI, the wins as well as the messy bits, and where they think things are heading next. It's on June 7th and 8th, and don't tell anyone, but we've got a really great deal for you. Scan this QR code to grab an early bird ticket for just £100. See you in London.

James: So that's an extreme example, I guess. Like most people aren't really running four different code reviewers on every PR, but even with one review bot, you can kind of see the same sort of issues being raised on each round.

So it's worded slightly differently and each time they're worded differently, the agent goes off and decides to try and implement whatever change that was asked for. So how do we fix this? First of all, recognizing that repetition. And then each finding that comes out of that repetition doesn't need to be a distinct action that needs to be taken.

So these kind of findings that happen in this review cycle need to be kind of aggregated against the existing findings that that bot or other bots have found within the PR. We should also look at making sure we've got consistent standards between all these different agents on these different pieces within our factory pipeline. We do this via skills and things like obviously your AGENTS.md or your CLAUDE.md. And making sure that what you think is good is clearly defined.

And every agent that is working in that repo understands that as well. And then finally allowing a human to jump in as well. So having some kind of condition, we'll talk about stop conditions shortly, but having some kind of condition that will detect this and then say, hey, this is not good, and pull in a human to ask for change or changing the scope, whatever makes sense there. So that's convergence.

Duplicate work and recovery

Next up is duplicate work and how we recover from duplicate work. So if we think about our factory it's effectively a distributed state machine. But it's also running across multiple third-party systems that you don't own. Right. So if you think about it, we have tickets in Linear. We have our kind of cloud execution environments, those sandboxes. We have our PRs on GitHub. We have CI runs.

We have review comments. We have things being merged. We have agent logs. All of these different elements are all distributed for most people anyway. And to kind of calculate our view of the world, we need to look at all of these things to understand what is happening. Luckily, none of this stuff is like new in terms of system design, right? Like, we've been building fault-tolerant distributed systems for a while now, and so we can kind of go back to first principles and ensure things like atomicity and idempotency are kind of part of our system design and the way we think about our factory.

That makes them fault-tolerant. Things are going to break. Yeah. This stuff is so, so hard to test, like, without using production. Like, you know, how do you mock GitHub, for example, or like, or Linear? Like you just can't do these things. And so things will definitely break.

So how do you recover from those? So I want to tell you a quick story about an issue we had that caused us a bunch of problems where a comment on a PR got counted twice and two different workers responded. Which we didn't initially notice. Sometimes the later worker could work out that the work was already being done and did nothing. There was like a no op, nothing happened there. But sometimes, depending on timing, the second worker could then also do some work and also react to those changes.

And obviously the kind of output that comes out of that is going to be different. Right. You give two agents the same task. They're never going to agree and do the same things. It's effectively nondeterminism and it's super hard to debug. We were testing with only a single worker. And obviously when there's a single worker you don't get into this state. And in prod, it was a very different story. In the end, we rewrote the queue entirely to handle this. So, we defined what was kind of a logical piece of work and which worker currently owned that. The team also did formal verification, which I'm not an expert in, to verify that the rebuilt queue did what we needed it to do.

Budgets and stop conditions

So fifth piece here is around control and budgets. So, actually stopping when things are going crazy. So we've got another PR again. The work done here, unlike the last PR that we looked at, is much more complex. The last one was just adding a field to an API result. This is a bunch of new functionality being added to our feature [name unclear, captioned as “verifies”]. So it ends up running over six days.

No one really was like keeping an eye on this and racked up $800 spend in tokens. And then the worst thing is it didn't even get merged, right? We just closed it because it was a bunch of slop. And if you thought 105 comments were bad [106 in the earlier example], this one had 533. So it was going crazy. So all those comments, all that conversation was basically a bunch of bots, including an agent that was running on a developer's machine that was watching the PR as well.

So what happened here? What was the mistake we made? Well, we were kind of like, not entirely oblivious to the fact that this might happen, right? We weren't just going to give a bunch of bots access to GitHub and say, go crazy, right? So we built in this limit of ten kind of bot interactions in a row, and we thought ten was a nice number. We thought, sure, that would make sense. And this was actually in the code.

This wasn't just context. The agent can work its way around that. This is like a physical restriction that was hard-coded. And so we were detecting in the threads within GitHub who's a bot who's a human and kind of making sure that everything was being adhered to. But we had two issues here. One was that logic was flawed, whether the user was a bot or not.

Nothing particularly amazing here. It was just a simple logic error. And so whenever the bot posted a comment, it was able to reset that counter back to zero. And so that ended up reading obviously as human intent. And so we basically had no guardrails at that point. On top of this, we also had the developer who is kind of owning this was running an agent locally on the machine, as I said, but it was acting on their behalf as a human.

So it was posting into the PR, and it looked like a human to our systems, but obviously we know it wasn't a human. It was Claude watching the PR and chiming in and like, you know, pouring gasoline on the fire. Really. So yeah, this continued for six days, kind of unnoticed. And we fixed the issue with the bot detection, which was one way of fixing it.

What we actually want to do, and we haven't done this yet, is actually start thinking about a budget for a work item. So rather than thinking about those individual number of turns, actually thinking about what is this actually costing us? So looking at the cost of the tokens, looking at the cost of things like CI runs. And budgeting against that.

I think personally, if you've got a couple of bots or agents talking to each other and they have 40 turns of talking to each other, but the work that's coming out is good and it's under budget and it's only costing you $5, then that's fine, right? Like, why try and limit that sort of like level of interaction? But yeah, this is our kind of plan that we want to move to, but we're not quite there yet. So.

Key takeaways: tools built for humans

So some key takeaways. Most of everything that the factory is driving at the moment is designed for a human at the wheel. Right. So if you take a look at things like GitHub, for example, the way the GitHub Apps API is designed, they can't approve their own PRs. So we have a factory app, which is the thing that will create PRs and put labels on things and do all that kind of stuff, but it can't auto-approve its own PRs because of a limitation of the GitHub API.

They never designed it to think, “Oh, five or six agents will be running as part of this app installation, so we should enable that.” Things like CI, every push gets a full run. I'm sure most people just have CI set up this way. Just because it's the way we've always done it. We just, you know, if someone does a push or a commit, we just trigger a bunch of, like, automated processes.

Why not hand some of that stuff off to an agent and let it decide when it wants to run CI. I think these days the models are good enough that, you know, you could trust them to make a good judgment on that and maybe put in other protections around things like running CI on main, for example. Anthropic have done a bunch of this recently. They posted a blog post about this a couple of weeks ago. So definitely worth looking at.

And then things like issue trackers, right? Traditionally issue trackers just have like one assignee. Linear added the ability to delegate to an agent like last year maybe, which is super cool, but why not delegate to like three agents or, a mixture of those different kind of settings? Right. Like all these restrictions are because these tools and most of the tools we're using have been built on a world that was not designed for agents.

Right. And especially not many coding agents working in parallel at speed all the time. The next piece I want to talk about briefly is just around autonomy. So everything we talked about today allowed us to earn a level of trust in the factory. We didn't just turn it all on from day one and let it just do everything that I talked about. We kind of started small, right? We started with some small elements. And as we kind of gained confidence that the factory was competent at doing those things, we gave it more and more autonomy and we were able to kind of step back more. This means that we can start kind of shifting left and shifting right.

So in terms of shifting left, we are starting to be less involved in the code. We are doing more and more work in that kind of upfront ticket planning, but we could shift even further left. As an engineer, I can start taking on more of the kind of product manager roles. I could start getting my agent to connect to things like PostHog, which we use for product analytics and making decisions about, should we even build this feature? Does it make sense? Will anyone use it? And then on the right hand side, thinking about stuff after it gets deployed, like doing testing in QA, in prod things, or maybe updating docs, things that I don't want to do anymore. And then lastly:

What you do by instinct, always record it in context and make sure that agents have access to that context. Right. So things that you just do instinctively as a human. Make sure it's written down. Make sure it's in a tool or a skill. And the agents can kind of access that and use that as needed to solve the problem.

So you don't have to repeat yourself all the time. And that's it. Thank you. I'm not sure how we are on time. We're a little over, but we have a 30 minute coffee break right after this. So, guys, feel free to come up and ask some questions. Another round of applause. Please forgive me. One more thing. I've got to do a bit of a pitch. So we've obviously just launched our brand new software factory. Scan the QR code. If you go and sign up and use the email that you've registered with at DevCon, you will get $500 of Tessl credits. So basically free agent tokens and you can go and start just playing around with this. So, please have a go. Thanks, everyone.
aiSummary: Tessl 工程师 James Moss 用团队的真实故障说明，多个编程智能体并行工作时，为什么会覆盖彼此的改动、陷入审查循环，还可能把成本推高。
oneSentenceSummary: Tessl 工程师 James Moss 用团队的真实故障说明，多个编程智能体并行工作时，为什么会覆盖彼此的改动、陷入审查循环，还可能把成本推高。
summary: James Moss 回顾了 Tessl 软件工厂的演进。它最初跑在一名工程师的笔记本上，后来由不同智能体接手实现、审查和跟进 PR，从工单一路推进到合并。他说，同样规模的团队每周合并的 PR 数增至原来的 3.5 倍，同时提醒这个数字只能反映大致趋势。并行之后，原本无关的工单会在同一个数据库迁移文件上冲突，智能体也可能在变基时悄悄丢掉别人的改动，或改掉原本失败的测试。一个只加了一个 API 字段的 PR 在 23 小时内经历了 11 轮审查，另一个 PR 在 6 天里花了 800 美元的 token 费用，最后直接关闭。Moss 介绍了 Tessl 加上的防护，比如监控破坏性改动、明确队列任务的归属，以及如何让审查意见去重。他也提出按工单核算 token 和 CI 开销，让人在工作迟迟没有进展时介入。

mainPoints.point: 并行改代码前，先找出共用的状态
mainPoints.explanation: 两个工单改的是不同的数据库模式，但 Drizzle 把两项迁移记在同一个 JSON 日志里。Tessl 把模式变更提前，并给智能体提供处理迁移冲突的指引。

mainPoints.point: 留意智能体在变基时做了什么
mainPoints.explanation: 有些智能体解决冲突时，会悄悄删掉自己开工后别人合入的代码，有时还会修改因此失败的测试。Tessl 在 PR 流程里加上了监控，发现这类改动后要求撤回。

mainPoints.point: 让每轮代码审查都离合并更近
mainPoints.explanation: 多个审查智能体为一个 API 字段花了 23 小时，来回审查了 11 轮。Moss 建议合并重复意见，让各审查方采用同一套标准，并在流程卡住时让人介入。

mainPoints.point: 同一个事件只交给一个执行者
mainPoints.explanation: 在生产环境里，两名执行者可能同时响应同一条 PR 评论。重写后的队列明确了什么算一项任务，以及当前由谁负责。
有个 PR 花了 800 美元的 token 费用，最后也没合并。机器人发评论可能把计数归零，本机运行的智能体还会以开发者身份发言。Moss 建议按工单追踪实际的 token 和 CI 开销。

keyQuotes: 你凭直觉就会做的事，也要把它写进上下文，并确保智能体能看到。
